core: The ordered sequence of a U.S. criminal case from arrest to appeal, as a map a student can hold in memory
Arrest with a warrant and arrest without one, and the paperwork that follows (complaint, booking)
The prompt judicial probable-cause determination required by Gerstein v. Pugh (1975) and the 48-hour presumption of County of Riverside v. McLaughlin (1991)
The initial appearance: advice of the charge, advice of rights, the release-or-detain decision, and appointment of counsel
Rothgery v. Gillespie County (2008): the Sixth Amendment right to counsel attaches at the initial appearance
Charging by complaint, by information, and by grand jury indictment; grand jury size and the twelve-juror concurrence

The Fifth Amendment grand jury requirement applies to federal felony prosecutions and was held in Hurtado v. California (1884) not to be required of the states by the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause
Preliminary hearing: function, timing, and Coleman v. Alabama (1970) treating it as a critical stage for right-to-counsel purposes
Arraignment and the entry of a plea; the conditional plea
Discovery under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 16 and the separate constitutional duty of Brady v. Maryland (1963), extended to impeachment evidence by Giglio v. United States (1972)
Pretrial motions, especially the motion to suppress, and the Rule 12 timing structure
Trial, verdict, post-trial motions (Rules 29 and 33), sentencing (Rule 32), and appeal
The distinction between direct appeal and collateral review (habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. 2254 and the 2255 motion)
Speedy Trial Act clocks: 30 days from arrest to charge, 70 days from charge or first appearance to trial, a 30-day floor before trial, excludable delay, and the dismissal sanction
That the overwhelming majority of cases resolve without trial, and that terminology and timing vary substantially by state
supporting: Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 5(f), which requires the judge to remind prosecutors of the Brady obligation on the record
California Constitution article I, section 14, as a concrete example of a state that permits felony prosecution by information after a magistrate's examination
USSC Sourcebook fiscal year 2025 Table 12 as the current dated federal plea-versus-trial figure
BJS's statement that there is no single U.S. criminal justice system

claims.claim: The Fourth Amendment requires a judicial determination of probable cause as a prerequisite to extended restraint of liberty following a warrantless arrest; the prosecutor's own assessment of probable cause does not satisfy it.

That probable-cause determination may be made by a judicial officer without an adversary hearing, and because of its limited function and nonadversary character it is not a critical stage of the prosecution that would require appointed counsel.

In County of Riverside v. McLaughlin (1991), decided May 13, 1991 in an opinion by Justice O'Connor joined by four other Justices, the Court held that a jurisdiction combining the probable-cause determination with other pretrial proceedings must do so as soon as reasonably feasible and in no event later than 48 hours after arrest; within 48 hours the arrested person must prove unreasonable delay, and beyond 48 hours the burden shifts to the government to show a bona fide emergency or other extraordinary circumstance, which cannot include intervening weekends.

Under the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure a complaint is a written statement of the essential facts constituting the offense, made under oath before a magistrate judge; a judge must issue an arrest warrant if the complaint or supporting affidavits establish probable cause; and a person arrested must be taken before a magistrate judge without unnecessary delay, with a complaint promptly filed when the arrest was warrantless.

At a federal initial appearance in a felony case the judge must inform the defendant of the complaint and any supporting affidavit, of the right to retain or request appointed counsel, of the circumstances of any pretrial release, of any right to a preliminary hearing, and of the right not to make a statement; must allow reasonable opportunity to consult counsel; and must detain or release the defendant as provided by statute. A defendant may be asked to plead only under Rule 10.

Rothgery v. Gillespie County (2008) held that a defendant's initial appearance before a magistrate, where he learns the charge against him and his liberty is subject to restriction, marks the initiation of adversary judicial proceedings that trigger attachment of the Sixth Amendment right to counsel, and that attachment does not require a prosecutor's awareness or involvement.

A federal offense punishable by death or by imprisonment for more than one year must be prosecuted by indictment unless the defendant waives indictment in open court, in which case it may proceed by information; a federal grand jury has 16 to 23 members and may indict only if at least 12 jurors concur.
Grand jury proceedings are closed and secret; witnesses compelled to testify before a federal grand jury are not allowed to have an attorney present in the room.

Hurtado v. California, decided March 3, 1884, held that the words 'due process of law' in the Fourteenth Amendment do not necessarily require indictment by a grand jury in a state prosecution for murder, so states may charge felonies by information after examination and commitment by a magistrate; the Fifth Amendment grand jury requirement therefore binds the federal government but has never been incorporated against the states.

California's constitution permits felonies to be prosecuted either by indictment or, after examination and commitment by a magistrate, by information, and requires that a person charged by felony complaint be taken before a magistrate without unnecessary delay and informed of the right to counsel.

A federal preliminary hearing must be held within 14 days of the initial appearance if the defendant is in custody and within 21 days if not, and is excused if the defendant waives it, is indicted, or is charged by information; at the hearing the defendant may cross-examine adverse witnesses and introduce evidence but may not object that evidence was unlawfully acquired, and a finding of no probable cause requires dismissal of the complaint without barring later prosecution.

In Coleman v. Alabama (1970) the Court held that Alabama's preliminary hearing was a critical stage of the prosecution at which the accused was entitled to appointed counsel, though the Court fractured: Justice Brennan announced the judgment for a plurality, and Justices Black and Harlan concurred in the conclusion on their own reasoning.

A federal arraignment must be conducted in open court and consists of ensuring the defendant has a copy of the indictment or information, reading it or stating the substance of the charge, and then asking the defendant to plead; a defendant may plead not guilty, guilty, or, with the court's consent, nolo contendere, and with the consent of the court and the government may enter a conditional plea reserving the right to appeal a specified pretrial ruling.

Brady v. Maryland (1963) held that suppression by the prosecution of evidence favorable to an accused who has requested it violates due process where the evidence is material either to guilt or to punishment, irrespective of the good faith or bad faith of the prosecution.

Giglio v. United States (1972) applied that duty to evidence affecting a witness's credibility, holding that an undisclosed promise of leniency to the government's key witness required a new trial and that the prosecutor's office is an entity, so one attorney's promise binds the government even if the trial attorney did not know of it; a finding of materiality is still required.

Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 5(f) requires that, on the first scheduled court date when both prosecutor and defense counsel are present, the judge issue an oral and written order confirming the prosecutor's disclosure obligation under Brady v. Maryland and its progeny and the possible consequences of violating that order.

Rule 16 obliges the government, on the defendant's request, to permit inspection of documents and objects material to preparing the defense or that it intends to use in its case-in-chief, and to disclose examination and test results and written expert disclosures; Rule 12(b)(3) requires that suppression of evidence and several other defenses be raised by pretrial motion, with the court setting a deadline at or after arraignment and the start of trial serving as the default deadline.

The Speedy Trial Act requires that an information or indictment be filed within 30 days of arrest or service of a summons (extended by 30 days where no grand jury has been in session), that trial commence within 70 days of the filing and making public of the charge or the defendant's first appearance, whichever is later, and that trial not begin less than 30 days after the defendant first appears through counsel unless the defendant consents in writing.

18 U.S.C. 3161(h) excludes many periods from those clocks, including delay from any pretrial motion from filing through the conclusion of the hearing or other prompt disposition, competency proceedings, interlocutory appeals, and consideration of a proposed plea agreement; under 18 U.S.C. 3162 a violation results in dismissal, with the court deciding whether dismissal is with or without prejudice by weighing the seriousness of the offense, the circumstances leading to dismissal, and the impact of reprosecution.

After a guilty verdict a defendant may move for a judgment of acquittal within 14 days of the verdict or the jury's discharge, and may move for a new trial within 14 days on grounds other than newly discovered evidence or within 3 years on newly discovered evidence; a federal probation officer must ordinarily prepare a presentence report before sentencing, and after sentencing the court must advise the defendant of any right to appeal the conviction or the sentence.

Collateral review is a separate proceeding from direct appeal: a state prisoner's federal habeas petition under 28 U.S.C. 2254 generally requires exhaustion of state remedies and, for claims adjudicated on the merits in state court, relief only where the decision was contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established federal law as determined by the Supreme Court or rested on an unreasonable determination of the facts; a federal prisoner instead moves under 28 U.S.C. 2255 in the sentencing court, subject to a one-year limitation period.

Of the 66,662 individuals sentenced in the federal courts in fiscal year 2025, 65,099 (97.7 percent) were convicted on a guilty plea and 1,563 (2.3 percent) after trial, and the plea share varies by offense type, from 99.7 percent for immigration offenses to 74.8 percent for murder.
The federal judiciary's own public description states that more than 90 percent of defendants plead guilty rather than go to trial.

There is no single criminal justice system in the United States: BJS describes many similar but individually unique systems in which criminal cases may be handled differently in different jurisdictions, with the limits of official discretion varying from jurisdiction to jurisdiction; BJS's own sequence places the initial appearance, an optional preliminary hearing, a grand jury or information, and then arraignment in that order.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How large the non-trial share of criminal cases is
positions: USSC Sourcebook FY2025 Table 12: 97.7 percent of individuals sentenced in federal court were convicted by guilty plea.
The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts states more than 90 percent of defendants plead guilty rather than go to trial.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: These are not in conflict but they count different things. The USSC table has a denominator of people sentenced, so it excludes cases dismissed or ending in acquittal; the uscourts figure is a rounder public statement about defendants. The lesson gives the USSC figure with its denominator stated and its fiscal year named, and does not generalize either number to state courts, where no comparable current national count exists. The mechanics of why so few cases reach trial belong to the plea-bargaining topic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a preliminary hearing is a stage at which counsel is constitutionally required
positions: Coleman v. Alabama (1970) treated Alabama's preliminary hearing as a critical stage requiring appointed counsel.
Gerstein v. Pugh (1975) held the Fourth Amendment probable-cause determination is not a critical stage requiring counsel.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are correct because they concern different proceedings. Gerstein itself distinguishes them: the Fourth Amendment determination asks only whether there is probable cause to detain and can be made on informal, nonadversary proof, whereas the Alabama preliminary hearing was an adversary proceeding whose conduct could impair the defense on the merits. The lesson keeps the two hearings separate and says why, because students routinely merge them.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the sequence taught here describes state practice
positions: The federal sequence is fixed by the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure and the Speedy Trial Act and is precisely knowable.
BJS states there is no single U.S. criminal justice system, and state names, deadlines, and charging instruments differ.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the federal sequence as the worked model because it is written down and verifiable, labels it as federal, and states repeatedly that state terminology and deadlines vary. Hurtado and the California constitutional provision are used to show the variation concretely rather than as a general claim.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted nothing specific about criminal procedure; its entire body was subject-agnostic boilerplate ('Arrest Through Trial is a foundational concept', 'a label on a toolbox drawer') with no legal content to verify.
The draft's vocabulary entries ('context', 'evidence', 'application') were generic study-skills terms rather than procedural terms, and its definition of the topic was circular.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire draft with a sourced procedural sequence verified against the opinions, the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure (December 1, 2025 committee print), and the United States Code.
Added the Gerstein and McLaughlin framework, which the draft omitted entirely, and stated the 48-hour figure as a presumption with burdens running in both directions rather than as a deadline.
Stated the grand jury requirement as federal only, with Hurtado as the reason it does not bind the states, rather than describing indictment as a universal step.
Separated Brady and Giglio as a constitutional due process duty from Rule 16 discovery, which students commonly conflate.
Distinguished direct appeal from collateral review and named the governing statutes.
Added explicit handoffs to bail-and-pretrial-procedure, plea-bargaining, trial-and-sentencing, court-structure, and constitutional-protections so the lesson does not duplicate their material.

sourceRecords.title: Gerstein v. Pugh, 420 U.S. 103 (1975)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office, govinfo (United States Reports volume 420)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Bound-volume PDF downloaded and the text extracted and read locally. Supports: the Fourth Amendment requires a judicial determination of probable cause as a prerequisite to extended restraint of liberty following arrest (420 U.S. at 114); the prosecutor's own assessment does not satisfy it; the determination may be made without an adversary hearing on informal proof; and because of its limited function and nonadversary character it is not a critical stage requiring appointed counsel, which the opinion contrasts with the Alabama preliminary hearing in Coleman v. Alabama. Argued March 25, 1974, reargued October 21, 1974, decided February 18, 1975; opinion by Powell, J.

sourceRecords.title: County of Riverside v. McLaughlin, 500 U.S. 44 (1991)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office, govinfo (United States Reports volume 500)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Bound-volume PDF downloaded and the text extracted and read locally. Supports the 48-hour framework: a jurisdiction combining probable-cause determinations with other pretrial proceedings must do so as soon as reasonably feasible and no later than 48 hours after arrest; a hearing within 48 hours may still violate Gerstein if the arrested individual proves unreasonable delay; beyond 48 hours the burden shifts to the government to show a bona fide emergency or other extraordinary circumstance, which cannot include intervening weekends or the time needed to consolidate pretrial proceedings. Argued January 7, 1991, decided May 13, 1991; O'Connor, J., for the Court, joined by Rehnquist, C.J., White, Kennedy, and Souter, JJ.; Marshall and Scalia, JJ., dissenting separately.

sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright

sourceRecords.title: Brady v. Maryland, 373 U.S. 83 (1963)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office, govinfo (United States Reports volume 373)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Bound-volume PDF downloaded and read locally. Supports the holding that suppression by the prosecution of evidence favorable to an accused who has requested it violates due process where the evidence is material either to guilt or to punishment, irrespective of the good faith or bad faith of the prosecution, and the facts (a withheld companion statement admitting the actual killing, surfacing only after conviction and affirmance). sourceRecords.title: Giglio v. United States, 405 U.S. 150 (1972)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office, govinfo (United States Reports volume 405)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Bound-volume PDF downloaded and read locally. Supports: nondisclosure of evidence affecting a witness's credibility falls within the Brady rule when the reliability of the witness may be determinative of guilt or innocence; a finding of materiality is still required and a new trial is not automatic; and the prosecutor's office is an entity, so a promise of leniency made by one government attorney is attributable to the government even though the trial attorney did not know of it. Argued October 12, 1971; decided February 24, 1972; Burger, C.J., for the Court, with Powell and Rehnquist, JJ., taking no part.

sourceRecords.title: California Constitution, article I, section 14 (prosecution of felonies; taking before a magistrate)
sourceRecords.provider: California Legislative Information (Office of Legislative Counsel)
sourceRecords.license: State constitutional text; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Section text retrieved and read (the page requires the article and section query parameters; the retrieved text was extracted from the returned page). Supports: felonies shall be prosecuted as provided by law, either by indictment or, after examination and commitment by a magistrate, by information; and a person charged by felony complaint must be taken without unnecessary delay before a magistrate, who must give a copy of the complaint and inform the defendant of the right to counsel. Added November 5, 1974 by Proposition 7. Used as one concrete example of state variation, not as a claim about states generally.

sourceRecords.title: Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure (December 1, 2025)
sourceRecords.provider: Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts / U.S. House Committee on the Judiciary committee print
sourceRecords.license: Federal rules of procedure prescribed under the Rules Enabling Act; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: The December 1, 2025 committee print was downloaded and the rule text extracted and read locally. Supports the federal procedural sequence: Rule 3 (complaint), Rule 4(a) (arrest warrant or summons on a showing of probable cause), Rule 5 (initial appearance without unnecessary delay, felony advice of rights, detention or release, plea only under Rule 10), Rule 5(f) (the on-the-record Brady reminder order), Rule 5.1 (preliminary hearing, 14 days in custody / 21 days out, cross-examination permitted, no suppression objections, dismissal on no probable cause without bar to later prosecution), Rule 6(a) and 6(f) (grand jury of 16 to 23 members, at least 12 concurring), Rule 7(a)-(b) (indictment required for offenses punishable by death or more than one year unless waived), Rule 10 (arraignment), Rule 11(a) (available pleas and the conditional plea), Rule 12(b)-(c) (pretrial motions, including suppression, and deadlines), Rule 16(a)(1)(E)-(G) (discovery of documents, examination results, and expert disclosures), Rule 29 (judgment of acquittal, 14 days after verdict), Rule 32(c) and 32(j) (presentence investigation; advice of the right to appeal), and Rule 33 (new trial, 14 days or 3 years for newly discovered evidence).

sourceRecords.title: 18 U.S.C. 3162 - Sanctions
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives (uscode.house.gov)
sourceRecords.license: United States Code; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Section text retrieved and read directly. Supports: a charge not filed within the section 3161(b) limit shall be dismissed or otherwise dropped; a defendant not brought to trial within the section 3161(c) limit is entitled to dismissal on motion; the court chooses dismissal with or without prejudice by weighing the seriousness of the offense, the facts and circumstances leading to dismissal, and the impact of reprosecution on the administration of justice; and failure to move before trial or before a guilty or nolo plea waives the right to dismissal.
